checklist.evidence: The draft says CSS has a native `token()` function in every current browser. No such CSS function exists. The code block also declares tokens with `$name:` instead of `--name:`.
Practical and friendly, no hype, no vendor comparisons.
The brief asks for a short code example, and the only CSS example is invalid and contradicts the React example. The takeaways, the original angle and the common mistakes are all covered.
The `token()` claim is false and has no source. The other claims are supported.
Inferred audience is community (peer front-end lead). The article is peer level with real code and trade-offs, and does not drift to a CTO or business reader.
The title promises why small teams should adopt tokens. The intro sets up exactly that with the forty-file scenario.
The title, the forty-file hook and the conclusion read as one complete thought.
The conclusion calls back to the forty-file green but leans on recap, and 'a naming problem' is a loose label for what is really duplication.
Sentences are clean, with no run-ons or stray capitals found.
`$color-primary: #0a5c36;` is not valid CSS custom property syntax, and `token()` does not exist. The React snippet uses `var(--color-surface)`, which the CSS block never defines.
No flagged words and 0 em dashes found. The language is plain.
Five genuine next-step FAQ questions, descriptive sentence-case headings, and the main claim appears early. The post is short enough that a TLDR is optional.
The reference page is the MDN custom properties guide. The article adds a repeat-count adoption rule, a mistakes list and a cost framing, though the CSS section is mostly MDN-level.
Quotable insight: 'The repeat count and the planned changes decide the payoff, not the size of the company.' It is reasoned, not experience-based, so it is only moderately strong.
The reader leaves with a clear adoption rule, a starting plan and a list of mistakes. The payoff is weakened by the broken code.

V3: 0 problematic passives; the article addresses the reader as you.

issues.anchor: CSS now has a native `token()` function in every current browser, so no `var()` is needed:
issues.description: CSS has no native `token()` function. Custom properties are read with `var(--name)`, as the draft's own cited MDN source says. This invented API contradicts the article's own claim and its earlier prose. Delete the claim and the `token()` usage, and use `var(--color-primary)`.

Custom properties must be declared with a `--` prefix (`--color-primary: #0a5c36;`). The `$` syntax is Sass, not CSS, so the block does not work as shown. The same applies to the dark theme override. Rewrite the block with `--` names and `background: var(--color-primary)`.

The React example reads `--color-surface` and `--space-4`, but the CSS block defines `$`-prefixed names and uses `token()`. The two samples disagree, so the prose and code do not match. Make both use the same `--` variables.

This negative, defensive heading leads with the problem. Rewrite it as 'Plan for the indirection. Tokens add a lookup step, and browser dev tools show the computed value to help you debug.' The other negatively framed bullets could be flipped the same way.

issues.anchor: The repeat count and the planned changes decide the payoff, not the size of the company.
issues.description: The angle is sound, but it rests on a general cost argument with no worked example. Add a small before-and-after, such as how many edits one rebrand takes with and without tokens, built from reasoning and not from invented numbers.

issues.anchor: The forty-file search for one green is a naming problem, and tokens fix it at any team size.
issues.description: The conclusion recaps the body steps and ends on a generic one-line edit. Call back to the three slightly different greens, then end on one idea to keep, for example: tokens record why a value exists, not only where it lives.

issues.anchor: Check every text and background pair against the WCAG minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for body text.
issues.description: The WCAG 4.5:1 figure and the W3C DTCG claim are correct, but they are not linked inline. Add inline links to the WCAG contrast criterion and the DTCG announcement.

technical_accuracy.evidence: The invented `token()` function and the `$` custom property syntax are wrong, even though the DTCG, WCAG and var() fallback claims are right.

technical_depth.evidence: The adoption rule and trade-offs are reasonable, but the implementation depth is undermined by the broken code.

practical_usefulness.evidence: A reader who copies the CSS example gets nothing that works. The adoption guidance and mistakes list are useful.

originality.evidence: The repeat-count rule is a clear angle, but it has no worked example and no hands-on specifics.

structure_clarity.evidence: The progression is logical and the headings are descriptive; the conclusion is slightly recap-like.

examples_implementation.evidence: The CSS sample is invalid, and the CSS and React samples contradict each other.

tradeoffs_limitations.evidence: The article covers runtime resolution, silent typo failures, indirection and when to wait.

references_support.evidence: The references are valid and relevant, but the WCAG and DTCG claims are not linked inline.

seo.evidence: The primary keyword is in the title, headings, slug and description; the secondary keywords are present.

audience_fit.evidence: The article is written at peer level for front-end leads, and the broken sample would cost it some credibility.

factual_correctness.evidence: CSS has no native `token()` function, and the draft's code uses non-CSS `$` custom property syntax. Both are material errors in the headline example.

claim_checks.claim: CSS now has a native `token()` function in every current browser, so no `var()` is needed
claim_checks.evidence: Custom properties are read with var(); MDN documents no token() function in CSS. The claim also contradicts the draft's own statement that tokens are read with var().

claim_checks.claim: CSS custom properties are declared with a -- prefix and read with var(), and they cascade and inherit
The W3C Design Tokens Community Group published the first stable version (2025.10) of its format in October 2025; it is a Community Group specification, not a W3C Standard
claim_checks.evidence: The DTCG announced the 2025.10 stable version on 28 October 2025. It is a Community Group report, not a W3C Recommendation.

claim_checks.claim: WCAG minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for body text
claim_checks.evidence: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 for normal text.

claim_checks.claim: A var() that points at an undefined property makes the declaration invalid at computed-value time
claim_checks.evidence: This is the documented behavior; the property falls back to its inherited or initial value.

summary: Scorecard: checks 1-5, 7 and 9-12 pass; check 6 (code) fails; check 8 (fact-check) fails; check 4 and V1/V2 pass with MEDIUM issues. Gate answers: the article earns the read through a concrete adoption rule and a relatable duplication hook, and it is worth writing for the 'tokens are only for big orgs' angle. The core CSS example is invalid and cites an invented `token()` function, so the article needs a fix before it can ship.
